words.name: >number
words.stack: ud1 c-addr1 u1 -- ud2 c-addr2 u2
words.doc: Attempt to convert the character string @var{c-addr1 u1} to an unsigned number in the current number base. The double @var{ud1} accumulates the result of the conversion to form @var{ud2}. Conversion continues, left-to-right, until the whole string is converted or a character that is not convertable in the current number base is encountered (including + or -). For each convertable character, @var{ud1} is first multiplied by the value in @code{BASE} and then incremented by the value represented by the character. @var{c-addr2} is the location of the first unconverted character (past the end of the string if the whole string was converted). @var{u2} is the number of unconverted characters in the string. Overflow is not detected.

words.name: catch
words.stack: x1 .. xn xt -- y1 .. ym 0 / z1 .. zn error
words.doc: @code{Executes} @i{xt}.  If execution returns normally, @code{catch} pushes 0 on the stack.  If execution returns through @code{throw}, all the stacks are reset to the depth on entry to @code{catch}, and the TOS (the @i{xt} position) is replaced with the throw code.

words.name: throw
words.stack: y1 .. ym nerror -- y1 .. ym / z1 .. zn error
words.doc: If @i{nerror} is 0, drop it and continue.  Otherwise, transfer control to the next dynamically enclosing exception handler, reset the stacks accordingly, and push @i{nerror}.

words.name: abort

Initialise/clear the pictured numeric output string.

Complete the pictured numeric output string by discarding @var{xd} and returning @var{addr u}; the address and length of the formatted string. A Standard program may modify characters within the string.

Start a hold area that ends with @code{#>>}. Can be nested in each other and in @code{<#}.  Note: if you do not match up the @code{<<#}s with @code{#>>}s, you will eventually run out of hold area; you can reset the hold area to empty with @code{<#}.
Release the hold area started with @code{<<#}.

words.name: sign
words.doc: Used within @code{<#} and @code{#>}. If @var{n} (a @var{single} number) is negative, append the display code for a minus sign to the pictured numeric output string. Since the string is built up ``backwards'' this is usually used immediately prior to @code{#>}, as shown in the examples below.

Used within @code{<#} and @code{#>}. Add the next least-significant digit to the pictured numeric output string. This is achieved by dividing @var{ud1} by the number in @code{base} to leave quotient @var{ud2} and remainder @var{n}; @var{n} is converted to the appropriate display code (eg ASCII code) and appended to the string. If the number has been fully converted, @var{ud1} will be 0 and @code{#} will append a ``0'' to the string.

words.name: #s
words.doc: Used within @code{<#} and @code{#>}. Convert all remaining digits using the same algorithm as for @code{#}. @code{#s} will convert at least one digit. Therefore, if @var{ud} is 0, @code{#s} will append a ``0'' to the pictured numeric output string.

If the definition is found return 1 (if the definition has non-default compilation semantics) or -1 (if the definition has default compilation semantics).  The @i{xt} returned in interpret state represents the interpretation semantics.  The @i{xt} returned in compile state represented either the compilation semantics (for non-default compilation semantics) or the run-time semantics that the compilation semantics would @code{compile,} (for default compilation semantics).  The ANS Forth standard does not specify clearly what the returned @i{xt} represents (and also talks about immediacy instead of non-default compilation semantics), so this word is questionable in portable programs. If non-portability is ok, @code{find-name} and friends are better (@pxref{Name token}).

When the input source is a text file, attempt to read the next line from the file. If successful, make the result the current input buffer, set @code{>IN} to 0 and return true; otherwise, return false.  A successful result includes receipt of a line containing 0 characters.

words.name: create-input
words.doc: create a new terminal input

words.name: execute-parsing
words.doc: Make @i{addr u} the current input source, execute @i{xt @code{( ... -- ... )}}, then restore the previous input source.

words.name: evaluate
words.doc: Save the current input source specification. Store @code{-1} in @code{source-id} and @code{0} in @code{blk}. Set @code{>IN} to @code{0} and make the string @i{c-addr u} the input source and input buffer. Interpret. When the parse area is empty, restore the input source specification.

words.name: clear-tibstack
words.doc: clears the tibstack; if there is none, create the bottom entry: the terminal input buffer.

words.name: query
words.doc: Make the user input device the input source. Receive input into the Terminal Input Buffer. Set @code{>IN} to zero. OBSOLESCENT: superceeded by @code{accept}.

words.name: line-end-hook
words.doc: called at every end-of-line when text-interpreting from a file

words.name: read-loop
words.doc: refill and interpret a file until EOF

words.name: execute-parsing-named-file
words.stack: i*x wfileid filename-addr filename-u xt -- j*x

words.name: execute-parsing-file
words.doc: Make @i{fileid} the current input source, execute @i{xt @code{( i*x -- j*x )}}, then restore the previous input source.

words.name: include-file
words.doc: Interpret (process using the text interpreter) the contents of the file @var{wfileid}.

words.name: xemit
words.doc: Prints an xchar on the terminal.

words.name: xkey
words.doc: Reads an xchar from the terminal. This will discard all input events up to the completion of the xchar.

words.name: xchar+
words.doc: Adds the size of the xchar stored at @var{xc-addr1} to this address, giving @var{xc-addr2}.

words.name: xchar-
words.doc: Goes backward from @var{xc_addr1} until it finds an xchar so that the size of this xchar added to @var{xc_addr2} gives @var{xc_addr1}.

words.name: +x/string
words.doc: Step forward by one xchar in the buffer defined by address @var{xc-addr1}, size @var{u1} pchars. @var{xc-addr2} is the address and u2 the size in pchars of the remaining buffer after stepping over the first xchar in the buffer.

words.name: x\string-
words.doc: Step backward by one xchar in the buffer defined by address @var{xc-addr1} and size @var{u1} in pchars, starting at the end of the buffer. @var{xc-addr1} is the address and @var{u2} the size in pchars of the remaining buffer after stepping backward over the last xchar in the buffer.

words.name: xc@
words.doc: Fetchs the xchar @var{xc} at @var{xc-addr1}.

words.name: xc!+?
words.stack: xc xc-addr1 u1 -- xc-addr2 u2 f
words.doc: Stores the xchar @var{xc} into the buffer starting at address @var{xc-addr1}, @var{u1} pchars large. @var{xc-addr2} points to the first memory location after @var{xc}, @var{u2} is the remaining size of the buffer. If the xchar @var{xc} did fit into the buffer, @var{f} is true, otherwise @var{f} is false, and @var{xc-addr2} @var{u2} equal @var{xc-addr1} @var{u1}. XC!+?  is safe for buffer overflows, and therefore preferred over XC!+.

words.name: xc@+
words.doc: Fetchs the xchar @var{xc} at @var{xc-addr1}. @var{xc-addr2} points to the first memory location after @var{xc}.

words.name: xc-size
words.doc: Computes the memory size of the xchar @var{xc} in pchars.

words.name: x-size
words.doc: Computes the memory size of the first xchar stored at @var{xc-addr} in pchars.

words.name: x-width
words.doc: @var{n} is the number of monospace ASCII pchars that take the same space to display as the the xchar string starting at @var{xc-addr}, using @var{u} pchars; assuming a monospaced display font, i.e. pchar width is always an integer multiple of the width of an ASCII pchar.

words.name: -trailing-garbage
words.doc: Examine the last XCHAR in the buffer @var{xc-addr} @var{u1}---if the encoding is correct and it repesents a full pchar, @var{u2} equals @var{u1}, otherwise, @var{u2} represents the string without the last (garbled) xchar.

words.name: xhold
words.doc: Put xc into the pictured numeric output

words.name: c!+?
words.stack: c c-addr1 u1 -- c-addr2 u2 f

words.name: arg
words.doc: Return the string for the @i{u}th command-line argument; returns @code{0 0} if the access is beyond the last argument.  @code{0 arg} is the program name with which you started Gforth.  The next unprocessed argument is always @code{1 arg}, the one after that is @code{2 arg} etc.  All arguments already processed by the system are deleted.  After you have processed an argument, you can delete it with @code{shift-args}.
An alias for @code{\}

words.name: pathdirs
words.tail_comment: dir string array, pointer and count

words.name: argv
words.doc: @code{Variable} -- a pointer to a vector of pointers to the command-line arguments (including the command-name). Each argument is represented as a C-style zero-terminated string.  Changed by @code{next-arg} and @code{shift-args}.

words.name: argc
words.doc: @code{Variable} -- the number of command-line arguments (including the command name).  Changed by @code{next-arg} and @code{shift-args}.

words.name: shift-args
words.doc: @code{1 arg} is deleted, shifting all following OS command line parameters to the left by 1, and reducing @code{argc @@}.  This word can change @code{argv @@}.

words.name: next-arg
words.doc: get the next argument from the OS command line, consuming it; if there is no argument left, return @code{0 0}.

words.name: path-allot
words.doc: @code{Allot} a path with @i{umax} characters capacity, initially empty.

words.name: also-path
words.doc: add the directory @i{c-addr len} to @i{path-addr}.

words.name: clear-path
words.doc: Set the path @i{path-addr} to empty.

words.name: path+
words.doc: Add the directory @var{dir} to the search path @var{path-addr}.

words.name: fpath+
words.doc: Add directory @var{dir} to the Forth search path.

words.name: path=
words.doc: Make a complete new search path; the path separator is |.

words.name: fpath=
words.doc: Make a complete new Forth search path; the path separator is |.

words.name: next-path
words.stack: addr u -- addr1 u1 addr2 u2

words.name: .path
words.doc: Display the contents of the search path @var{path-addr}.

words.name: .fpath
words.doc: Display the contents of the Forth search path.

words.name: absolut-path?
words.doc: A path is absolute if it starts with a / or a ~ (~ expansion), or if it is in the form ./*, extended regexp: ^[/~]|./, or if it has a colon as second character ("C:...").  Paths simply containing a / are not absolute!

words.name: open-ofile
words.doc: opens the file whose name is in ofile

words.name: check-path
words.stack: adr1 len1 adr2 len2 -- fid 0 | 0 ior

words.name: open-path-file
words.stack: addr1 u1 path-addr -- wfileid addr2 u2 0 | ior
words.doc: Look in path @var{path-addr} for the file specified by @var{addr1 u1}.  If found, the resulting path and and (read-only) open file descriptor are returned. If the file is not found, @var{ior} is what came back from the last attempt at opening the file (in the current implementation).

words.name: open-fpath-file
words.stack: addr1 u1 -- wfileid addr2 u2 0 | ior
words.doc: Look in the Forth search path for the file specified by @var{addr1 u1}. If found, the resulting path and an open file descriptor are returned. If the file is not found, @var{ior} is non-zero.

words.name: sourcefilename
words.doc: The name of the source file which is currently the input source.  The result is valid only while the file is being loaded.  If the current input source is no (stream) file, the result is undefined.  In Gforth, the result is valid during the whole seesion (but not across @code{savesystem} etc.).

words.name: sourceline#
words.doc: The line number of the line that is currently being interpreted from a (stream) file. The first line has the number 1. If the current input source is not a (stream) file, the result is undefined.

words.name: included?
words.doc: True only if the file @var{c-addr u} is in the list of earlier included files. If the file has been loaded, it may have been specified as, say, @file{foo.fs} and found somewhere on the Forth search path. To return @code{true} from @code{included?}, you must specify the exact path to the file, even if that is @file{./foo.fs}

words.name: add-included-file
words.doc: add name c-addr u to included-files

words.name: included1
words.doc: Include the file file-id with the name given by @var{c-addr u}.

words.name: included
words.doc: @code{include-file} the file whose name is given by the string @var{c-addr u}.

words.name: required
words.doc: @code{include-file} the file with the name given by @var{addr u}, if it is not @code{included} (or @code{required}) already. Currently this works by comparing the name of the file (with path) against the names of earlier included files.

words.name: include
words.doc: @code{include-file} the file @var{file}.

words.name: require
words.doc: @code{include-file} @var{file} only if it is not included already.

words.name: .strings
words.doc: list the strings from an array of string descriptors at addr with u entries, one per line.

words.name: .included
words.doc: list the names of the files that have been @code{included}

words.name: locals-list
words.tail_comment: acts like a variable that contains

words.name: dead-code
words.tail_comment: true if normal code at "here" would be dead

words.name: dest
words.tail_comment: the loopback branch is always assumed live

words.name: ?DUP-IF
words.doc: This is the preferred alternative to the idiom "@code{?DUP IF}", since it can be better handled by tools like stack checkers. Besides, it's faster.

words.name: WHILE
words.stack: compilation dest -- orig dest ; run-time f --

words.name: DO
words.stack: compilation -- do-sys ; run-time w1 w2 -- loop-sys

words.name: ?DO
words.stack: compilation -- do-sys ; run-time w1 w2 -- | loop-sys

words.name: +DO
words.stack: compilation -- do-sys ; run-time n1 n2 -- | loop-sys

words.name: U+DO
words.stack: compilation -- do-sys ; run-time u1 u2 -- | loop-sys

words.name: -DO
words.stack: compilation -- do-sys ; run-time n1 n2 -- | loop-sys

words.name: U-DO
words.stack: compilation -- do-sys ; run-time u1 u2 -- | loop-sys

words.name: +LOOP
words.stack: compilation do-sys -- ; run-time loop-sys1 n -- | loop-sys2

words.name: -LOOP
words.stack: compilation do-sys -- ; run-time loop-sys1 u -- | loop-sys2

words.name: S+LOOP
words.stack: compilation do-sys -- ; run-time loop-sys1 n -- | loop-sys2

words.name: EXIT
words.doc: Return to the calling definition; usually used as a way of forcing an early return from a definition. Before @code{EXIT}ing you must clean up the return stack and @code{UNLOOP} any outstanding @code{?DO}...@code{LOOP}s.

words.name: SLiteral
words.stack: Compilation c-addr1 u ; run-time -- c-addr2 u
words.doc: Compilation: compile the string specified by @i{c-addr1}, @i{u} into the current definition. Run-time: return @i{c-addr2 u} describing the address and length of the string.

words.name: abort"
words.doc: If any bit of @i{f} is non-zero, perform the function of @code{-2 throw}, displaying the string @i{ccc} if there is no exception frame on the exception stack.

words.name: S"
words.doc: Compilation: Parse a string @i{ccc} delimited by a @code{"} (double quote). At run-time, return the length, @i{u}, and the start address, @i{c-addr} of the string. Interpretation: parse the string as before, and return @i{c-addr}, @i{u}. Gforth @code{allocate}s the string. The resulting memory leak is usually not a problem; the exception is if you create strings containing @code{S"} and @code{evaluate} them; then the leak is not bounded by the size of the interpreted files and you may want to @code{free} the strings.  ANS Forth only guarantees one buffer of 80 characters, so in standard programs you should assume that the string lives only until the next @code{s"}.

Compilation: Parse a string @i{ccc} delimited by a " (double quote). At run-time, display the string. Interpretation semantics for this word are undefined in ANS Forth. Gforth's interpretation semantics are to display the string. This is the simplest way to display a string from within a definition; see examples below.

words.name: [IF]
words.doc: If flag is @code{TRUE} do nothing (and therefore execute subsequent words as normal). If flag is @code{FALSE}, parse and discard words from the parse area (refilling it if necessary using @code{REFILL}) including nested instances of @code{[IF]}.. @code{[ELSE]}.. @code{[THEN]} and @code{[IF]}.. @code{[THEN]} until the balancing @code{[ELSE]} or @code{[THEN]} has been parsed and discarded. Immediate word.

words.name: [IFDEF]
words.doc: If name is found in the current search-order, behave like @code{[IF]} with a @code{TRUE} flag, otherwise behave like @code{[IF]} with a @code{FALSE} flag. Immediate word.

words.name: [IFUNDEF]
words.doc: If name is not found in the current search-order, behave like @code{[IF]} with a @code{TRUE} flag, otherwise behave like @code{[IF]} with a @code{FALSE} flag. Immediate word.

words.name: [ELSE]
words.doc: Parse and discard words from the parse area (refilling it if necessary using @code{REFILL}) including nested instances of @code{[IF]}.. @code{[ELSE]}.. @code{[THEN]} and @code{[IF]}.. @code{[THEN]} until the balancing @code{[THEN]} has been parsed and discarded. @code{[ELSE]} only gets executed if the balancing @code{[IF]} was @code{TRUE}; if it was @code{FALSE}, @code{[IF]} would have parsed and discarded the @code{[ELSE]}, leaving the subsequent words to be executed as normal. Immediate word.

words.name: [THEN]
words.doc: Do nothing; used as a marker for other words to parse and discard up to. Immediate word.

words.name: [ENDIF]
words.doc: Do nothing; synonym for @code{[THEN]}

words.name: maxdepth-.s
words.doc: A variable containing 9 by default.  @code{.s} and @code{f.s} display at most that many stack items.

words.name: .s
words.doc: Display the number of items on the data stack, followed by a list of the items (but not more than specified by @code{maxdepth-.s}; TOS is the right-most item.

words.name: dump
words.doc: Display @var{u} lines of memory starting at address @var{addr}. Each line displays the contents of 16 bytes. When Gforth is running under an operating system you may get @file{Invalid memory address} errors if you attempt to access arbitrary locations.
Display the contents of address @var{a-addr} in the current number base.

words.name: wordlist-words
words.doc: Display the contents of the wordlist wid.

words.name: words
words.doc: ** this will not get annotated. See other defn in search.fs .. ** It does not work to use "wordset-" prefix since this file is glossed by cross.fs which doesn't have the same functionalty as makedoc.fs

words.name: vlist
words.doc: Old (pre-Forth-83) name for @code{WORDS}.

words.name: docon:
words.doc: The code address of a @code{CONSTANT}.

words.name: dovalue:
words.doc: The code address of a @code{CONSTANT}.

words.name: docol:
words.doc: The code address of a colon definition.

words.name: dovar:
words.doc: The code address of a @code{CREATE}d word.

words.name: douser:
words.doc: The code address of a @code{USER} variable.

words.name: dodefer:
words.doc: The code address of a @code{defer}ed word.

words.name: dofield:
words.doc: The code address of a @code{field}.

words.name: dodoes:
words.doc: The code address of a @code{field}???

words.name: nothrow
words.doc: Use this (or the standard sequence @code{['] false catch drop}) after a @code{catch} or @code{endtry} that does not rethrow; this ensures that the next @code{throw} will record a backtrace.

words.name: try
words.doc: Start an exception-catching region.

words.name: iferror
words.doc: Starts the exception handling code (executed if there is an exception between @code{try} and @code{endtry}).  This part has to be finished with @code{then}.

words.name: restore
words.doc: Starts restoring code, that is executed if there is an exception, and if there is no exception.

words.name: endtry
words.doc: End an exception-catching region.

words.name: endtry-iferror
words.doc: End an exception-catching region while starting exception-handling code outside that region (executed if there is an exception between @code{try} and @code{endtry-iferror}). This part has to be finished with @code{then} (or @code{else}...@code{then}).

words.name: naligned
words.doc: @var{addr2} is the aligned version of @var{addr1} with respect to the alignment @var{n}.

words.name: field,
words.stack: align1 offset1 align size --  align2 offset2

words.name: create-field
words.stack: align1 offset1 align size --  align2 offset2

words.name: field
words.stack: align1 offset1 align size "name" --  align2 offset2
words.doc: Create a field @var{name} with offset @var{offset1}, and the type given by @var{align size}. @var{offset2} is the offset of the next field, and @var{align2} is the alignment of all fields.@* @code{name} execution: @var{addr1} -- @var{addr2}.@* @var{addr2}=@var{addr1}+@var{offset1}

words.name: end-struct
words.doc: Define a structure/type descriptor @var{name} with alignment @var{align} and size @var{size1} (@var{size} rounded up to be a multiple of @var{align}).@* @code{name} execution: -- @var{align size1}@*

words.name: struct
words.doc: An empty structure, used to start a structure definition.

words.name: %alignment
words.doc: The alignment of the structure.

words.name: %size
words.doc: The size of the structure.

words.name: %align
words.doc: Align the data space pointer to the alignment @var{align}.

words.name: %allot
words.doc: Allot @var{size} address units of data space with alignment @var{align}; the resulting block of data is found at @var{addr}.

words.name: %allocate
words.doc: Allocate @var{size} address units with alignment @var{align}, similar to @code{allocate}.

words.name: %alloc
words.doc: Allocate @var{size} address units with alignment @var{align}, giving a data block at @var{addr}; @code{throw} an ior code if not successful.

words.name: maxvp
words.tail_comment: current size of search order stack

words.name: maxvp-limit
words.tail_comment: upper limit for resizing search order stack

words.name: get-current
words.doc: @i{wid} is the identifier of the current compilation word list.

words.name: set-current
words.doc: Set the compilation word list to the word list identified by @i{wid}.

words.name: definitions
words.doc: Set the compilation word list to be the same as the word list that is currently at the top of the search order.

words.name: mappedwordlist
words.doc: Create a wordlist with a special map-structure.

words.name: wordlist
words.doc: Create a new, empty word list represented by @i{wid}.

words.name: Vocabulary
words.doc: Create a definition "name" and associate a new word list with it. The run-time effect of "name" is to replace the @i{wid} at the top of the search order with the @i{wid} associated with the new word list.

words.name: >order
words.doc: Push @var{wid} on the search order.

words.name: also
words.doc: Like @code{DUP} for the search order. Usually used before a vocabulary (e.g., @code{also Forth}); the combined effect is to push the wordlist represented by the vocabulary on the search order.

words.name: previous
words.doc: Drop the wordlist at the top of the search order.

words.name: Forth
words.doc: Replace the @i{wid} at the top of the search order with the @i{wid} associated with the word list @code{forth-wordlist}.

words.name: Root
words.doc: Add the root wordlist to the search order stack.  This vocabulary makes up the minimum search order and contains only a search-order words.

words.name: Only
words.doc: Set the search order to the implementation-defined minimum search order (for Gforth, this is the word list @code{Root}).

words.name: get-order
words.doc: Copy the search order to the data stack. The current search order has @i{n} entries, of which @i{wid1} represents the wordlist that is searched first (the word list at the top of the search order) and @i{widn} represents the wordlist that is searched last.

words.name: set-order
words.doc: If @var{n}=0, empty the search order.  If @var{n}=-1, set the search order to the implementation-defined minimum search order (for Gforth, this is the word list @code{Root}). Otherwise, replace the existing search order with the @var{n} wid entries such that @var{wid1} represents the word list that will be searched first and @var{widn} represents the word list that will be searched last.

words.name: seal
words.doc: Remove all word lists from the search order stack other than the word list that is currently on the top of the search order stack.

words.name: id.
words.doc: Print the name of the word represented by @var{nt}.

words.name: .id
words.doc: F83 name for @code{id.}.

words.name: .name
words.doc: Gforth <=0.5.0 name for @code{id.}.

words.name: .voc
words.doc: print the name of the wordlist represented by @var{wid}.  Can only print names defined with @code{vocabulary} or @code{wordlist constant}, otherwise prints @samp{???}.

words.name: order
words.doc: Print the search order and the compilation word list.  The word lists are printed in the order in which they are searched (which is reversed with respect to the conventional way of displaying stacks). The compilation word list is displayed last.

words.name: vocs
words.doc: List vocabularies and wordlists defined in the system.

words.name: words
words.doc: Display a list of all of the definitions in the word list at the top of the search order.

words.name: forth-wordlist
words.doc: @code{Constant} -- @i{wid} identifies the word list that includes all of the standard words provided by Gforth. When Gforth is invoked, this word list is the compilation word list and is at the top of the search order.

words.name: environment-wordlist
words.doc: @i{wid} identifies the word list that is searched by environmental queries.

words.name: environment?
words.doc: @i{c-addr, u} specify a counted string. If the string is not recognised, return a @code{false} flag. Otherwise return a @code{true} flag and some (string-specific) information about the queried string.

words.name: ADDRESS-UNIT-BITS
words.doc: Size of one address unit, in bits.

words.name: MAX-CHAR
words.doc: Maximum value of any character in the character set

words.name: /COUNTED-STRING
words.doc: Maximum size of a counted string, in characters.

words.name: /HOLD
words.doc: Size of the pictured numeric string output buffer, in characters.

words.name: /PAD
words.doc: Size of the scratch area pointed to by @code{PAD}, in characters.

words.name: CORE
words.doc: True if the complete core word set is present. Always true for Gforth.

words.name: CORE-EXT
words.doc: True if the complete core extension word set is present. Always true for Gforth.

words.name: FLOORED
words.doc: True if @code{/} etc. perform floored division

words.name: MAX-N
words.doc: Largest usable signed integer.

words.name: MAX-U
words.doc: Largest usable unsigned integer.

words.name: MAX-D
words.doc: Largest usable signed double.

words.name: MAX-UD
words.doc: Largest usable unsigned double.

words.name: gforth
words.doc: Counted string representing a version string for this version of Gforth (for versions>0.3.0).  The version strings of the various versions are guaranteed to be ordered lexicographically.

words.name: return-stack-cells
words.doc: Maximum size of the return stack, in cells.

words.name: stack-cells
words.doc: Maximum size of the data stack, in cells.

words.name: floating-stack
words.doc: @var{n} is non-zero, showing that Gforth maintains a separate floating-point stack of depth @var{n}.

words.name: os-class
words.doc: Counted string representing a description of the host operating system.

words.name: os-type
words.doc: Counted string equal to "$host_os"

words.name: libtool-command
words.doc: name of the GNU libtool command

words.name: libtool-cc
words.doc: invocation string of the C compiler used for libtool

words.name: libtool-flags
words.doc: force no undefined for cygwin

words.name: exception
words.doc: @var{n} is a previously unused @code{throw} value in the range (-4095...-256). Consecutive calls to @code{exception} return consecutive decreasing numbers. Gforth uses the string @var{addr u} as an error message.

words.name: broken-pipe-error
words.doc: the error number for a broken pipe

Compilation and interpretation semantics: Parse a string @i{ccc} delimited by a @code{)} (right parenthesis). Display the string. This is often used to display progress information during compilation; see examples below.

words.name: m*/
words.doc: dquot=(d1*n2)/u3, with the intermediate result being triple-precision. In ANS Forth u3 can only be a positive signed number.

words.name: C"
words.doc: Compilation: parse a string @i{ccc} delimited by a @code{"} (double quote). At run-time, return @i{c-addr} which specifies the counted string @i{ccc}.  Interpretation semantics are undefined.

words.name: convert
words.doc: Obsolescent: superseded by @code{>number}.

words.name: erase
words.doc: Clear all bits in @i{u} aus starting at @i{addr}.

words.name: blank
words.doc: Store the space character into @i{u} chars starting at @i{c-addr}.

words.name: search
words.stack: c-addr1 u1 c-addr2 u2 -- c-addr3 u3 flag
words.doc: Search the string specified by @i{c-addr1, u1} for the string specified by @i{c-addr2, u2}. If @i{flag} is true: match was found at @i{c-addr3} with @i{u3} characters remaining. If @i{flag} is false: no match was found; @i{c-addr3, u3} are equal to @i{c-addr1, u1}.

words.name: span
words.doc: @code{Variable} -- @i{c-addr} is the address of a cell that stores the length of the last string received by @code{expect}. OBSOLESCENT.

words.name: expect
words.doc: Receive a string of at most @i{+n} characters, and store it in memory starting at @i{c-addr}. The string is displayed. Input terminates when the <return> key is pressed or @i{+n} characters have been received. The normal Gforth line editing capabilites are available. The length of the string is stored in @code{span}; it does not include the <return> character. OBSOLESCENT: superceeded by @code{accept}.

words.name: marker
words.doc: Create a definition, @i{name} (called a @i{mark}) whose execution semantics are to remove itself and everything defined after it.

words.name: sfalign
words.doc: If the data-space pointer is not single-float-aligned, reserve enough space to align it.

words.name: f.rdp
words.doc: Print float @i{rf} formatted.  The total width of the output is @i{nr}.  For fixed-point notation, the number of digits after the decimal point is @i{+nd} and the minimum number of significant digits is @i{np}.  @code{Set-precision} has no effect on @code{f.rdp}.  Fixed-point notation is used if the number of siginicant digits would be at least @i{np} and if the number of digits before the decimal point would fit.  If fixed-point notation is not used, exponential notation is used, and if that does not fit, asterisks are printed.  We recommend using @i{nr}>=7 to avoid the risk of numbers not fitting at all.  We recommend @i{nr}>=@i{np}+5 to avoid cases where @code{f.rdp} switches to exponential notation because fixed-point notation would have too few significant digits, yet exponential notation offers fewer significant digits.  We recommend @i{nr}>=@i{nd}+2, if you want to have fixed-point notation for some numbers.  We recommend @i{np}>@i{nr}, if you want to have exponential notation for all numbers.
